title: Financial Management and Commitment to Sending Remittances of Filipina Wives in Virginia, United States
venue: Journal of Family Sciences, Vol. 10, No. 1
tldr: Filipina wives in Virginia manage household finances through clear goals, working budgets, and savings, while maintaining commitment to sending monthly remittances that support their Philippine-based families of orientation.
problem_and_motivation: There is a dearth of research on the financial management of Filipina wives with their family of procreation living overseas who simultaneously send remittances to their family of orientation in the Philippines. Understanding how these women balance household budgeting, savings, and remittance commitments is critical for designing interventions that support their financial wellbeing.
approach: Qualitative case study with nine Filipina wives residing in Virginia, USA, using purposive and snowball sampling.
Face-to-face in-depth interviews conducted during 2018-2020, supplemented by follow-up video calls for financial details.
Interview schedule covering socio-demographics, migration history, income patterns, expenditure patterns, and remittance practices.
Thematic analysis using within-case and across-case analysis to derive themes from participant responses.
Data validated by three faculty experts on family studies; transcripts coded using description-focused and interpretation-focused strategies.
findings: All nine households practice financial management with clear goals, working monthly budgets, and savings.
Not all participants are in the labor force; some are dependent homemakers on sole-earner husbands.
Monthly household income ranges from $5,000 to $22,500 depending on dual or single income sources.
All participants send regular monthly remittances ranging from $100 to $800+ to families in the Philippines.
Emergency remittance requests from family of origin pose risk to household budget and savings stability.
Most households aim to save approximately $1,000 monthly after all financial obligations.
Financial decision-making is predominantly joint between couples, with husbands as primary budget holders in most American-Filipina households.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This qualitative study provides rich empirical data on the financial management practices of Filipina migrant wives, a demographic underrepresented in financial behavior research. It reveals how cultural values of utang-na-loob and family-centeredness shape financial decision-making and remittance commitments in transnational households. The study documents the tension between maintaining household financial stability in the US and fulfilling obligations to family of orientation in the Philippines. It contributes to understanding how migration status, gender roles, and cultural obligations interact to influence personal financial management strategies.
directly_justifies: All participants maintain working monthly budgets and savings despite dual-family financial obligations.
Emergency remittance requests pose significant risk to household budget and savings stability.
Filipino cultural values of utang-na-loob directly drive remittance commitment regardless of income level.
Financial decision-making in most households is joint, with both spouses contributing to budget management.
limits: Numerical data are participant estimations rather than actual verified values.
Study limited to Virginia, limiting generalizability to all Filipina wives in the US.
Small sample size of nine participants reduces statistical representativeness.
Data collection period of 2018-2020 may not reflect current economic conditions.
topic_relevance.topic_relevance: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned. Domain 2.A (Culturally Specific Financial Practices) received high relevance as the paper directly addresses Filipino cultural values driving financial behavior. Domains 1.B and 1.C received medium relevance due to examination of financial structure and behavior, though participants are Filipina wives rather than young professionals per se. Domains 4.A and 4.B received low relevance due to brief discussion of existing financial systems. Domains 3, 5-14 were considered and rejected: the paper does not address expense categorization frameworks, behavioral profiling, predictive modeling, budgeting strategies as algorithms, anomaly detection, mobile design, privacy, engagement, evaluation frameworks, savings/debt management systems, or synthetic data generation. The paper's primary contribution is qualitative financial behavior documentation rather than system design.

limitations: Numerical data are participant estimations, not actual verified financial records.
Study limited to Virginia, preventing generalization to all Filipina wives in the US.
Small sample size of nine participants reduces statistical representativeness.
Data collected during 2018-2020 may not reflect current economic conditions.
Husbands were not interviewed, limiting perspectives on financial management. [unacknowledged]
